title: Diagnosing Personalization Failures in Mobile GUI Agents

paper.title: Diagnosing Personalization Failures in Mobile GUI Agents
paper.abstract:
Abstract Unlike conventional GUI agents,
personalized GUI agents require user preferences to guide a sequential execution policy over changing GUI states.
This creates two challenges for the agentic design: 1) Determining HOW each preference should alter the agent’s execution strategy. 2) Determining WHEN each preference should take effect along the interaction trajectory.
However, existing benchmarks primarily evaluate overall task success only, making it difficult to evaluate agents’ reasoning ability to determine HOW and WHEN preferences should affect execution.
To address this, we introduce PrefDiag-Bench with two key components: 1) a categorization of user preferences into five types, characterizing HOW they affect agent execution; and 2) a stage-wise diagnostic framework with 1,664 probes, tracing WHEN preferences should take effect along the interaction trajectory and where failures occur.
Experimentally, we evaluate eleven GUI agent systems, including end-to-end agents and agentic workflows, under two forms of user context: explicit user profiles and behavioral memory logs.
We find while existing GUI agents achieve relatively high task completion rates on non-personalized tasks, their performance remains substantially lower on preference-personalized tasks.
Even the best-performing model, Seed-2.0-Pro, achieves only 47.17% on process preferences under explicit user profiles. Moreover, agents struggle particularly with Ranking and Process preferences, indicating substantial room for improvement.
Further analysis reveals two key capability bottlenecks behind these failures: selecting relevant evidence from user history, and recognizing when user preferences should take effect during execution. Controlled interventions that explicitly provide relevant evidence improve end-to-end task success by up to 7.06%.
We hope PrefDiag-Bench can provide a more systematic and comprehensive evaluation of GUI agents’ personalization capabilities, moving beyond simply measuring overall task success. All code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Zhixin-L/PrefDiag-Bench .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Recent mobile GUI agents powered by large language models (LLMs) have made substantial progress in GUI perception, task planning, and task execution in real-world applications, bringing them closer to personalized assistants. In such a personalization setting, simply completing a user request is no longer sufficient; agents also are required to draw on users’ past behavior, habits, and preferences to make decisions that meet individual needs during execution. For example, for the same base task “order a milk tea according to my usual preferences and add it to the cart” the agent may need to select the preferred drink options, satisfy a price constraint, prioritize a store with faster delivery, or compare multiple candidates. Therefore, the same GUI task may impose different execution requirements under different user preferences. The example above highlights two challenges for personalized GUI agents. First, an agent is required to determine HOW each preference should alter execution: it may change the desired outcome, restrict valid choices, change candidate priorities, or constrain the execution process or interaction behavior. Second, the agent is required to determine WHEN a preference should take effect along the interaction trajectory, based on the current task and GUI state. Figure 1 illustrates these two complementary challenges: preferences impose distinct execution requirements, while a task-relevant preference should only be applied when its trigger state is reached. These challenges require evaluation beyond task completion. A benchmark should assess whether an agent can determine HOW a preference should alter execution and WHEN it should take effect, while also identifying where failures arise along the path from user context to GUI actions. Existing evaluations centered on task-level success or preference-sensitive progress provide limited information about this process. To address these challenges from a data-centric perspective, we introduce PrefDiag-Bench, a fine-grained diagnostic benchmark for personalized GUI agents. PrefDiag-Bench contains two complementary components corresponding to the challenges above. First, while the benchmark spans diverse application domains, including shopping, workflow, and transportation, its main evaluation axis is the primary effect of each preference on agent execution. We organize user preferences into five execution-oriented types, i.e. , Outcome, Constraint, Ranking, Process, and Interaction—characterizing HOW they affect agent execution, and construct corresponding end-to-end tasks to compare agents under different execution requirements. Second, we develop a stage-wise diagnostic framework that covers three high-level phases, i.e. , information processing, contextual reasoning, and action formulation, and further divides them into five diagnostic stages. The framework probes the capabilities required to apply preferences from user context to GUI actions, including recognizing WHEN a preference should take effect, and identifies capability bottlenecks arise during personalized execution. Figure 1 : Motivation for PrefDiag-Bench. Top: Different user preferences impose distinct execution requirements on mobile GUI agents, affecting desired outcomes, feasible choices, candidate priorities, execution procedures, and user interaction. Bottom: The interaction example illustrates that knowing a task-relevant preference is insufficient: the agent must also recognize the appropriate GUI state in which to apply it. PrefDiag-Bench complements end-to-end evaluation with stage-wise diagnostic probes across information processing, contextual reasoning, and action formulation to identify capability gaps in preference application. Based on this design, PrefDiag-Bench contains 318 end-to-end GUI tasks and 1,664 associated diagnostic probes. Each end-to-end task is paired with a set of diagnostic probes built around the same underlying preference instance. This paired design allows us not only to evaluate whether an agent completes the task while satisfying the user’s preference in an interactive GUI environment, but also to connect end-to-end performance with specific diagnostic stages. In addition, we construct explicit user profiles and behavioral memory logs as two user-context representations at different levels of abstraction, enabling us to study how the form of user context affects personalized execution. Experimentally, we systematically evaluate 11 existing popular personalized GUI agentic designs, including nine end-to-end agents and two agentic workflows, M3A and T3A, using explicit user profiles and behavioral memory logs. Our results indicate three main findings. First, performance varies substantially across the five preference types, showing that collapsing performance across preference types into a single aggregate score can obscure important capability differences. Second, explicit user profiles do not consistently outperform behavioral memory logs, suggesting that compact preference summaries are not always more useful than logs that retain concrete behavioral evidence. Third, selecting relevant evidence from user history and recognizing when preferences should take effect emerge as the two main bottlenecks. Controlled interventions on a representative subset of systems further show that explicit evidence guidance improves end-to-end task success by up to 7.06 percentage points, demonstrating that evidence selection has a measurable impact on personalized execution and provides a concrete target for system improvement.

sections.heading: 2.1 Mobile GUI Agents and Their Personalized Evaluation
sections.text: Recent mobile GUI agents have made substantial progress in GUI perception, task planning, and multi-step task execution \citep liu2025llmpoweredguiagentsphone,nguyen-etal-2025-gui,hu-etal-2025-os. Existing systems include agent frameworks that organize task execution through explicit reasoning and control modules, such as AppAgent \citep ZhangYLLHCHF025, M3A \citep ICLR2025_01a83bc2, and Mobile-Agent-v3 \citep ye2025mobileagentv3fundamentalagentsgui, as well as end-to-end agents that directly generate reasoning traces and actions from GUI observations, such as UI-TARS \citep qin2025ui and GUI-Owl \citep ye2025mobileagentv3fundamentalagentsgui. As the GUI capabilities of these systems continue to improve, recent studies have begun to examine how agents can use user history and preferences to adapt their behavior during task execution. PersonalAlign \citep lyu-etal-2026-personalalign uses long-term user records to recover preferences omitted from vague instructions; PSPA-Bench \citep nie2026pspabenchpersonalizedbenchmarksmartphone decomposes tasks to evaluate preference-sensitive progress; KnowU-Bench \citep chen2026knowubenchinteractiveproactivepersonalized uses behavioral logs to assess preference inference, user clarification, and proactive decision-making; and Persona2Web \citep kim2026persona2webbenchmarkingpersonalizedweb studies contextual reasoning from long-term user histories in web environments. These studies broaden personalized agent evaluation from complementary directions. However, they do not jointly examine how different preferences affect GUI execution or which capabilities become bottlenecks when preferences are applied from user context to GUI actions. PrefDiag-Bench complements this line of work with an execution-oriented and stage-wise diagnostic perspective.

sections.heading: 2.2 Personalization User Context and Memory
sections.text: Personalization relies on memory as a key source of user context, allowing agents to retain and reuse information from past interactions \citep zhang2025tmlr-personalization,liu2025surveypersonalizedlargelanguage. Memory systems such as MemoryBank \citep DBLP:conf/aaai/ZhongGGYW24 and Mem0 \citep ChhikaraKASY25 extract, update, and retrieve user information from ongoing interactions to support long-term personalization. Corresponding benchmarks examine this process from different perspectives. PersonaMem \citep JHCLYCea25 evaluates whether models can track evolving user profiles from multi-session interaction histories and generate personalized responses accordingly. AlpsBench \citep Xiao_2026 decomposes personalized memory management into information extraction, updating, retrieval, and utilization. In mobile GUI environments, MemGUI-Bench \citep liu2026memguibenchbenchmarkingmemorymobile focuses on memory retention and use across steps, applications, and sessions.However, correctly inferring or retrieving user information does not necessarily mean that an agent can apply user preferences correctly in a GUI task. Personalized GUI agents must further connect user context with the current task and GUI state, and translate relevant preferences into concrete behaviors such as candidate selection, ranking, process control, or user interaction. PrefDiag-Bench complements these studies by comparing explicit user profiles and behavioral memory logs in GUI tasks and probing capability gaps from user-context processing to action formulation.

sections.heading: 3.1 Preference Taxonomy
sections.text: User preferences concern different application domains and semantic content. For mobile GUI agents, however, a more direct distinction is the type of decision that each preference changes during task execution. We therefore use preferences’ primary effects on execution as our main evaluation axis, classifying each preference by the part of a personalized task’s success criterion that it directly changes. This yields five types, illustrated in Figure 1 . Specifically, as shown in the Figure 1 , Outcome preference specifies the desired outcome or final choice, such as selecting “no sugar” and “less ice” in a drink-ordering task. A Constraint preference sets conditions that a valid outcome or allowed action must satisfy, such as keeping the drink price at or below 20$. A Ranking preference specifies priorities among valid candidates, rather than determining whether a candidate satisfies a hard constraint. For example, when several stores offer the target drink, the agent should prioritize the store with the shortest delivery time and choose the cheaper store when delivery times are equal. A Process preference specifies how a task should be carried out, such as comparing the price of the same product across multiple platforms before making a choice. The final GUI state alone is insufficient to verify this requirement: the execution trajectory must also show that the prescribed procedure was followed. An Interaction preference specifies whether, when, and how the agent should interact with the user. For example, after finding a suitable item, the agent should request confirmation and add it to the cart only after the user agrees. Although both types affect the interaction trajectory, Process constrains the task procedure, whereas Interaction constrains communication with the user. A task may therefore reach the expected final state yet still violate its preference requirements if a required comparison or confirmation was skipped during execution.

sections.heading: 3.2 Benchmark Overview and Statistics
sections.text: PrefDiag-Bench evaluates agents’ ability to apply user preferences across diverse mobile tasks. It comprises 53 task families, each with one Basic task and five preference-conditioned variants, yielding 318 instances (53 Basic and 265 personalized). As shown in Figure 2 (a), the tasks span seven application domains: communication, office, commerce, navigation, system settings, information retrieval, and social media. Within the diagnostic set, preference atoms also cover nine semantic categories, including workflow, user control, time and context, resource limits, and safety and privacy (Figure 2 (c)). These categories describe what preferences concern, complementing the taxonomy that distinguishes how they alter agent behavior. Formally, we define a personalized instance as 𝒯 i = ( I i , C i , E i 0 , S i ) \mathcal{T}_{i}=(I_{i},C_{i},E_{i}^{0},S_{i}) , where I i I_{i} is the instruction, C i C_{i} is the user context conveying preference p i p_{i} , E i 0 E_{i}^{0} is the initial environment state, and S i S_{i} is a deterministic success checker. The agent is required to identify the relevant preference requirements from C i C_{i} and complete the task while satisfying all of them at the appropriate stages of execution. Execution produces a trajectory τ i = ( o 1 , a 1 , … , o T , a T ) \tau_{i}=(o_{1},a_{1},\ldots,o_{T},a_{T}) of observations and actions. The checker evaluates the final state E i T E_{i}^{T} and relevant action or user–agent interaction records, returning S i ​ ( E i T , τ i ) ∈ { 0 , 1 } S_{i}(E_{i}^{T},\tau_{i})\in\{0,1\} . A result of 1 requires satisfying both the task goal and all preference-specific requirements, including any prescribed procedure or confirmation. To examine the capabilities underlying these task outcomes, we include 1,664 diagnostic probes associated with 260 preference atoms from 256 tasks with observed failures under behavioral logs (Figure 2 (b)). Each atom is the smallest preference requirement that can be diagnosed and applied independently. Across information processing, contextual reasoning, and action formulation, the probes test preference induction from logs (P1), evidence selection for a given preference (P2), task relevance (P3), state-level trigger recognition (P4), and semantic action selection for an active preference (P5). They are evaluated independently, with ground-truth prerequisites supplied when needed; This pairing connects task outcomes with tests of specific capabilities rather than describing personalization only through aggregate task success. sections.heading: 3.3 Data Construction and Annotation
sections.text: We construct preference-conditioned variants from selected KnowU-Bench tasks \citep chen2026knowubenchinteractiveproactivepersonalized, inspecting their goals, application settings, and success criteria. Every resulting variant is manually reviewed. The target preference is conveyed through user context rather than restated in the instruction. We construct paired contexts by first drafting explicit user profiles with an LLM, revising and checking them with GPT-5.6 Sol, and reviewing every profile manually. Synthetic behavioral memory logs are then generated from the reviewed profiles, with four to five profile-related entries per collection, and undergo the same model-assisted revision and human review. The underlying preference, instruction, initial environment state, and success checker remain fixed across the two context forms. We derive task-linked diagnostic probes from execution failures under behavioral logs, retaining cases with valid checker results and deduplicating them across agents by task. Independently diagnosable preference requirements are separated into atoms. Probe questions, options, and reference annotations are drafted with LLM assistance and revised by humans. For P4 and P5, we use atoms with clear trigger boundaries and usable reference trajectories. P5 reference actions are extracted from successful rollouts of the corresponding tasks and represented as semantic operations. Human reviewers answer all multiple-choice probes.

sections.heading: Evaluated Systems.
sections.text: We evaluate 11 systems. The closed-source agents are Seed-2.0-Pro \citep seed2026seed20modelcardintelligence, Claude Sonnet 4.6 \citep anthropic2026sonnet46, and Qwen3.7-Plus \citep alibaba2026qwen37plus. The open-source agents are MAI-UI-8B \citep zhou2025maiuitechnicalreportrealworld, Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking \citep abs-2511-21631, Step-GUI-4B \citep abs-2512-15431, GUI-Owl-1.5-8B-Instruct \citep xu2026mobileagentv35multiplatformfundamentalgui, and UI-Venus-1.5-8B \citep venusteam2026uivenus15technicalreport. We also evaluate two agentic workflows, M3A and T3A \citep ICLR2025_01a83bc2, both using GPT-5.4. Open-source models run on a server with eight NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs.

sections.heading: Evaluation Protocol.
sections.text: All 11 systems are evaluated on 53 Basic tasks and 265 preference-conditioned tasks, the latter under both explicit user profiles and behavioral memory logs. All systems share task environments and checkers while retaining their native observation and action interfaces. Instructions, initial states, and checkers remain fixed across profile–log pairs. We report Task Success Rate (TSR) by preference type and context form. Independent P1–P5 probes are applied to the nine directly queried agents; workflows are excluded to avoid assessing only their backbone or introducing workflow-specific probe adaptations. Diagnostic results are aggregated by task, preference, and probe type: a result is correct only if all associated items are answered correctly. We report accuracy per probe type and an overall score across all task-level diagnostic results.

sections.text: Table 2 reports TSR on the 53 Basic tasks and the 265 preference-conditioned tasks. For each personalized task, we compare explicit user profiles with behavioral memory logs while keeping the task instruction, initial environment state, and success checker fixed. The AVG columns report the macro-average over the five preference types.

sections.heading: Personalized tasks are more challenging to execute.
sections.text: All 11 systems achieve lower average TSR on preference-conditioned tasks than on Basic tasks under both forms of user context. Seed-2.0-Pro obtains the strongest personalized results, reaching 62.64% with explicit profiles and 65.66% with behavioral logs, compared with 81.13% on Basic . In contrast, Claude Sonnet 4.6 achieves the highest Basic TSR of 86.79%, but is surpassed by Seed-2.0-Pro under both personalized settings. This ranking change shows that strong general GUI execution is important, but is not sufficient for applying user preferences throughout a multi-step interaction trajectory. sections.heading: Different preference types expose distinct performance patterns.
sections.text: Outcome is the best-performing type for 10 of the 11 systems under explicit user profiles and for all 11 systems under behavioral memory logs. At the other end, Ranking and Process emerge as recurring difficulties across systems and user-context forms. Process is the lowest-performing type for seven systems under explicit profiles and the lowest or tied-lowest type for eight systems under behavioral memory logs. Under behavioral memory logs, Qwen3.7-Plus drops from 62.26% on Outcome to 16.98% on Process, a gap of 45.28 percentage points. Ranking remains difficult even for the strongest system: Seed-2.0-Pro achieves 83.02% on Outcome but only 45.28% on Ranking under behavioral memory logs, a difference of 37.74 points. These results show that reporting only an overall personalized score would hide major differences in the execution requirements that each system can handle. The repeated difficulty on Ranking and Process is consistent with the additional candidate comparison required by Ranking and the longer execution procedure required by Process.

sections.heading: More explicit user context is not always more effective.
sections.text: The profile–log comparison has no consistent direction across systems. Behavioral logs improve Seed-2.0-Pro from 62.64% to 65.66% and T3A from 24.91% to 29.44%, whereas M3A drops from 37.73% with profiles to 18.49% with logs. This contrast is notable because M3A and T3A use the same GPT-5.4 backbone, suggesting that the usefulness of a context form also depends on how the overall workflow processes user information. This pattern is consistent with the trade-off built into the two representations: profiles directly provide compact preference rules, whereas logs preserve concrete behavioral evidence but require the agent to identify which evidence is relevant. These task-level comparisons reveal performance gaps across execution requirements and context forms, but do not isolate the capabilities underlying preference application. We next examine these capabilities using independent probes constructed from failures under behavioral memory logs.

sections.heading: 4.3 Stage-Wise Diagnostic Results
sections.text: Figure 3 reports task-level accuracy on P2–P4 for the nine directly evaluated agents. P1 and P5 are omitted from the heatmaps because they are near ceiling for most systems, but are included in the aggregate statistics below.

sections.heading: Evidence selection and trigger recognition are the weakest measured stages.
sections.text: On the failure-derived diagnostic set, P2 Evidence Selection and P4 Trigger Recognition are the lowest-scoring stages across systems, averaging 40.06% and 39.69%, respectively, compared with 88.80% for P3 and over 98.9% for P1 and P5. Even Seed-2.0-Pro reaches only 71.48% on P2 and 58.14% on P4. Since both probes provide the target preference, these results highlight the need to improve agents’ ability to identify supporting evidence in user history and recognize when a known preference should take effect.

sections.heading: The Thinking variant stands out among open-source agents.
sections.text: Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking achieves the highest accuracy among the evaluated open-source agents on both P2 and P4. On P2, it scores 69.53%, compared with 21.88% for Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct; on P4, the corresponding scores are 45.79% and 25.58%. Its P2 accuracy also approaches the 71.48% achieved by Seed-2.0-Pro and Qwen3.7-Plus, narrowing the gap with the leading closed-source systems in evidence selection.These results suggest that the Thinking variant’s reasoning capabilities contribute to its higher accuracy in evidence selection and trigger recognition.

sections.heading: 4.4 Joint Analysis
sections.text: Figure 4 : Joint outcomes between end-to-end task execution and stage-wise diagnostic probes. For each system and diagnostic stage, we partition paired task-probe outcomes into four categories: TT (both pass), TF (the task passes / the probe fails), FT (the task fails / the probe passes), and FF (both fail). The distributions reveal how failures identified by individual diagnostic stages relate to failures in complete task execution. For each of the nine directly evaluated agents, we pair every task-level diagnostic result with the corresponding end-to-end outcome under behavioral memory logs. Since the diagnostic set is deduplicated across agents, a task included due to one agent’s failure may still be completed by another agent. Figure 4 partitions the eligible paired instances into four joint outcomes: both task and probe pass (TT), the task passes but the probe fails (TF), the task fails but the probe passes (FT), and both task and probe fail (FF).

sections.heading: P2 and P4 failures frequently co-occur with task failures.
sections.text: P2 Evidence Selection and P4 Trigger Recognition show markedly higher joint-failure proportions than the other diagnostic stages. Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct fails both the task and its associated probe on 65.5% of P2 pairs and 61.7% of P4 pairs. The corresponding proportions are 68.1% and 51.9% for GUI-Owl-1.5-8B-Instruct, and 82.1% and 66.0% for Step-GUI-4B. These results connect the weaknesses identified by the independent probes to failures on the corresponding GUI tasks, reinforcing evidence selection and trigger recognition as important targets for improvement.

sections.heading: 4.5 Controlled Evidence Intervention
sections.text: To test whether P2 Evidence Selection is an actionable bottleneck, we evaluate Seed-2.0-Pro, Qwen3.7-Plus, Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking, and Step-GUI-4B on a fixed subset of 85 tasks selected from the 265 preference-conditioned tasks. Table 3(a) compares three conditions: C0 Raw Logs uses the original logs; C1 Oracle Evidence Labels retains all entries and labels each as supporting or noise for the target preference, without changing its text or order; C2 Supporting Logs Only removes all noise entries and retains only supporting logs. C1 tests whether explicitly identifying supporting and noise logs helps execution, while C2 tests whether removing noise is more effective than retaining and labeling it. The task instruction, initial environment state, and success checker remain fixed.

sections.heading: Evidence labeling can outperform noise removal.
sections.text: From C0 to C1, Seed-2.0-Pro improves from 76.47% to 83.53%, a gain of 7.06 percentage points, and Qwen3.7-Plus improves from 50.59% to 56.47%. These gains show that explicitly distinguishing supporting logs from noise can help agents complete personalized tasks. However, replacing labeled logs with supporting-only logs (C2) reduces their TSR to 81.18% and 51.76%, respectively. For these systems, identifying which logs support the preference is therefore more effective than simply discarding the rest. A possible explanation is that labeled noise provides contrastive cues about which historical behaviors should not guide the current decision, whereas deleting these entries removes those cues.

sections.heading: Limited GUI capability may constrain intervention benefits.
sections.text: Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking achieves 69.53% on P2 and 45.79% on P4, but only 30.19% on Basic tasks and 12.07% on the full preference-conditioned set under behavioral logs (Table 2 ). On the 85-task intervention subset, its TSR remains low: 17.65% under C0, 16.47% under C1, and 18.82% under C2. This contrast suggests that limitations in GUI execution constrain the gains from evidence guidance, even when evidence selection is relatively strong. Step-GUI-4B also reaches only 18.82% under both C1 and C2. These results suggest that strong GUI execution is a necessary foundation for personalized task success: when an agent’s basic GUI capability is limited, even accurate preference understanding may not translate into successful end-to-end execution. sections.heading: 4.6 Robustness to Memory Construction Methods
sections.text: To test whether the preference-type differences in Section 4.2 depend on our original memory construction, we evaluate Seed-2.0-Pro on all 265 preference-conditioned tasks using alternative memory inputs produced by Mem0 \citep ChhikaraKASY25, LangMem \citep langchain2025langmem, and Hindsight \citep latimer-etal-2026-hindsight from the same source behavioral records. The task instruction, initial environment state, success checker, and execution settings remain fixed. Table 3(b) reports TSR by preference type, with the original behavioral memory logs included as Ours .

sections.heading: Preference-type differences persist across memory construction methods.
sections.text: Outcome remains the highest-scoring type, while Ranking and Process are the two lowest-scoring types under all three methods. With Mem0, TSR is 71.70% on Outcome, compared with 43.40% on Ranking and 50.94% on Process. Hindsight shows the same broad contrast, reaching 79.25% on Outcome, 45.28% on Ranking, and 37.74% on Process. Although the absolute scores and the ordering of Ranking and Process change, their relative difficulty persists across the tested methods. This consistency further supports our preference-conditioned task design, as the observed differences across preference types persist under alternative memory construction methods rather than being specific to our original behavioral memory logs.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduce PrefDiag-Bench to provide a more systematic and comprehensive view of personalization in mobile GUI agents. By categorizing user preferences into five types and combining this categorization with a stage-wise diagnostic framework, it examines how preferences affect agent execution, when they should take effect, and where capability gaps arise. Our evaluation shows that overall task success alone can obscure distinct strengths and weaknesses across preference types and stages of preference application. Connecting these capability-level assessments with end-to-end outcomes provides a basis for more informative evaluation and targeted interventions. We hope PrefDiag-Bench supports the development of GUI agents that not only understand user preferences but also apply them reliably throughout task execution.

sections.heading: A.2 User-Context Construction and Annotation
sections.text: Figure 5 summarizes the overall construction process. We detail below how explicit user profiles, behavioral memory logs, and their reference annotations are produced. Figure 5 : Construction pipeline of PrefDiag-Bench. Top: Task construction with paired profiles and behavioral logs. Bottom: Failure selection, preference-atom extraction, and diagnostic-probe construction. Both stages combine model-assisted drafting with human revision.

sections.heading: Profile drafting and review.
sections.text: For each personalized task, we specify the intended preference and its applicable conditions. An LLM drafts an explicit user profile, which GPT-5.6 Sol checks and revises before human reviewers examine every profile. Reviewers check the requested behavior, applicable conditions, and task-specific details against the intended preference. The reviewed profile then serves as the basis for log synthesis.

sections.heading: Behavioral-log synthesis.
sections.text: Using the reviewed profile, an LLM generates synthetic records of past choices, corrections, confirmations, and related activities. Supporting records provide evidence for the target preference, while distractors may share an application, product category, or recipient without establishing the same requirement. Contextual exceptions are retained where present. The logs undergo GPT-5.6 Sol revision and item-by-item human review alongside the profile. Reviewers check that both forms convey compatible requirements and that distractors remain plausible historical records rather than explicitly declaring their irrelevance. The instruction, initial environment state, and success checker remain fixed across the paired context forms.

sections.heading: Reference annotation and validation.
sections.text: We link each preference atom to its supporting log entries and annotate task applicability, trigger conditions, and the expected behavior for diagnostic construction. Reviewers check evidence support against the actual record content. For the confirmation example in Section A.2.1 , a recorded ask–confirm–submit sequence supports the preference, whereas store selection or price comparison does not. When inconsistencies are found, the source records are revised and the affected context pairs and probes are rechecked. Automated checks validate identifiers, required fields, and evidence references.

sections.heading: Environment and task inputs.
sections.text: We reuse the Android environment and evaluation infrastructure of KnowU-Bench, with task-specific initial data and checkers for PrefDiag-Bench. Each episode starts from its prescribed application state, with agent history reset between tasks. Episodes allow at most 65 environment steps with a one-second inter-step wait, and can end earlier when the agent reports completion or inability to proceed. Open-source models are served on eight NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs. The 53 Basic tasks receive no additional user context. Each of the 265 personalized tasks receives either its explicit user profile or its behavioral memory logs. The instruction and context remain available throughout execution, alongside the current observation, adapter-specific history, and any platform reply. Adapters retain native observation and action formats while mapping actions and coordinates to the common environment interface.

sections.heading: Decoding and workflow interfaces.
sections.text: The Qwen, MAI-UI, Step-GUI, GUI-Owl, and UI-Venus adapters use temperature 0. Seed-2.0-Pro uses temperature 0.7, top- p = 0.9 p=0.9 , and a 4,096-token response limit; its adapter retains the three most recent screenshots alongside textual history. Claude’s adapter does not explicitly set temperature. M3A and T3A use GPT-5.4 with temperature 0, a 2,048 token action-response limit, and up to 20 objective action summaries. Both workflows use the same task contexts, step budget, and checkers as the directly evaluated agents.

sections.heading: End-to-end success.
sections.text: Let r i ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] r_{i}\in[0,1] be the native checker score for task instance i i . Checkers inspect application state, database or callback records, and required action and interaction traces. Any accompanying natural-language reason is not used as a separate success classifier. The personalized AVG is the macro-average of the five preference-type TSRs.

sections.text: Each P1–P5 item is answered in an independent request, without passing model predictions between probes. Single-choice items require the reference option; P2 requires an exact match to the complete reference option set. For task–preference instance i i and probe type k k , let 𝒬 i , k \mathcal{Q}_{i,k} contain all associated canonical questions, including those from multiple atoms or GUI states. sections.heading: Paired outcomes.
sections.text: We join diagnostic and end-to-end results by model, task-family ID, and preference type. Each eligible pair contributes once per probe type. TT, TF, FT, and FF denote ( s i , a i , k ) = ( 1 , 1 ) , ( 1 , 0 ) , ( 0 , 1 ) , ( 0 , 0 ) (s_{i},a_{i,k})=(1,1),(1,0),(0,1),(0,0) , respectively. Pooled proportions are calculated from valid pair counts, not by averaging preference-wise percentages.

sections.heading: Task selection.
sections.text: The fixed subset contains 85 task–preference pairs from 43 families, with 17 pairs per preference type: 15 P2-target pairs, one downstream control, and one retention control. The totals are therefore 75, 5, and 5 pairs, respectively. Selection uses pre-intervention diagnostic and behavioral-log execution records. A P2-target pair requires at least one model that fails both P2 and the task, and at least one model that completes the task. Downstream controls have correct P2 answers but failed execution; retention controls have successful diagnostic and execution outcomes. Every selected pair has an audited supporting-log mapping and at least one distractor. This P2-enriched subset is shared across all four models and all conditions, and selection does not use intervention outcomes.

sections.text: C0 supplies the behavioral memory logs without evidence labels. Abstract Unlike conventional GUI agents, personalized GUI agents require user preferences to guide a sequential execution policy over changing GUI states. This creates two challenges for the agentic design: 1) Determining HOW each preference should alter the agent’s execution strategy. 2) Determining WHEN each preference should take effect along the interaction trajectory. However, existing benchmarks primarily evaluate overall task success only, making it difficult to evaluate agents’ reasoning ability to determine HOW and WHEN preferences should affect execution. To address this, we introduce PrefDiag-Bench with two key components: 1) a categorization of user preferences into five types, characterizing HOW they affect agent execution; and 2) a stage-wise diagnostic framework with 1,664 probes, tracing WHEN preferences should take effect along the interaction trajectory and where failures occur. Experimentally, we evaluate eleven GUI agent systems, including end-to-end agents and agentic workflows, under two forms of user context: explicit user profiles and behavioral memory logs. We find while existing GUI agents achieve relatively high task completion rates on non-personalized tasks, their performance remains substantially lower on preference-personalized tasks. Even the best-performing model, Seed-2.0-Pro, achieves only 47.17% on process preferences under explicit user profiles. Moreover, agents struggle particularly with Ranking and Process preferences, indicating substantial room for improvement. Further analysis reveals two key capability bottlenecks behind these failures: selecting relevant evidence from user history, and recognizing when user preferences should take effect during execution. Controlled interventions that explicitly provide relevant evidence improve end-to-end task success by up to 7.06%. We hope PrefDiag-Bench can provide a more systematic and comprehensive evaluation of GUI agents’ personalization capabilities, moving beyond simply measuring overall task success. All code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Zhixin-L/PrefDiag-Bench . \lhead Preprint † † footnotetext: Email: zxlin7488@gmail.com * * footnotetext: Correspondence to: Dongliang Xu (xudongliang@sdu.edu.cn); Yue Yao (yaoyorke@gmail.com). 1 Introduction Recent mobile GUI agents powered by large language models (LLMs) have made substantial progress in GUI perception, task planning, and task execution in real-world applications, bringing them closer to personalized assistants. In such a personalization setting, simply completing a user request is no longer sufficient; agents also are required to draw on users’ past behavior, habits, and preferences to make decisions that meet individual needs during execution. For example, for the same base task “order a milk tea according to my usual preferences and add it to the cart” the agent may need to select the preferred drink options, satisfy a price constraint, prioritize a store with faster delivery, or compare multiple candidates. Therefore, the same GUI task may impose different execution requirements under different user preferences. The example above highlights two challenges for personalized GUI agents. First, an agent is required to determine HOW each preference should alter execution: it may change the desired outcome, restrict valid choices, change candidate priorities, or constrain the execution process or interaction behavior. Second, the agent is required to determine WHEN a preference should take effect along the interaction trajectory, based on the current task and GUI state. Figure 1 illustrates these two complementary challenges: preferences impose distinct execution requirements, while a task-relevant preference should only be applied when its trigger state is reached. These challenges require evaluation beyond task completion. A benchmark should assess whether an agent can determine HOW a preference should alter execution and WHEN it should take effect, while also identifying where failures arise along the path from user context to GUI actions. Existing evaluations centered on task-level success or preference-sensitive progress provide limited information about this process. To address these challenges from a data-centric perspective, we introduce PrefDiag-Bench, a fine-grained diagnostic benchmark for personalized GUI agents. PrefDiag-Bench contains two complementary components corresponding to the challenges above. First, while the benchmark spans diverse application domains, including shopping, workflow, and transportation, its main evaluation axis is the primary effect of each preference on agent execution. We organize user preferences into five execution-oriented types, i.e. , Outcome, Constraint, Ranking, Process, and Interaction—characterizing HOW they affect agent execution, and construct corresponding end-to-end tasks to compare agents under different execution requirements. Second, we develop a stage-wise diagnostic framework that covers three high-level phases, i.e. , information processing, contextual reasoning, and action formulation, and further divides them into five diagnostic stages. The framework probes the capabilities required to apply preferences from user context to GUI actions, including recognizing WHEN a preference should take effect, and identifies capability bottlenecks arise during personalized execution. Figure 1 : Motivation for PrefDiag-Bench. Top: Different user preferences impose distinct execution requirements on mobile GUI agents, affecting desired outcomes, feasible choices, candidate priorities, execution procedures, and user interaction. Bottom: The interaction example illustrates that knowing a task-relevant preference is insufficient: the agent must also recognize the appropriate GUI state in which to apply it. PrefDiag-Bench complements end-to-end evaluation with stage-wise diagnostic probes across information processing, contextual reasoning, and action formulation to identify capability gaps in preference application. Based on this design, PrefDiag-Bench contains 318 end-to-end GUI tasks and 1,664 associated diagnostic probes. Each end-to-end task is paired with a set of diagnostic probes built around the same underlying preference instance. This paired design allows us not only to evaluate whether an agent completes the task while satisfying the user’s preference in an interactive GUI environment, but also to connect end-to-end performance with specific diagnostic stages. In addition, we construct explicit user profiles and behavioral memory logs as two user-context representations at different levels of abstraction, enabling us to study how the form of user context affects personalized execution. Experimentally, we systematically evaluate 11 existing popular personalized GUI agentic designs, including nine end-to-end agents and two agentic workflows, M3A and T3A, using explicit user profiles and behavioral memory logs. Our results indicate three main findings. First, performance varies substantially across the five preference types, showing that collapsing performance across preference types into a single aggregate score can obscure important capability differences. Second, explicit user profiles do not consistently outperform behavioral memory logs, suggesting that compact preference summaries are not always more useful than logs that retain concrete behavioral evidence. Third, selecting relevant evidence from user history and recognizing when preferences should take effect emerge as the two main bottlenecks. Controlled interventions on a representative subset of systems further show that explicit evidence guidance improves end-to-end task success by up to 7.06 percentage points, demonstrating that evidence selection has a measurable impact on personalized execution and provides a concrete target for system improvement. 2 Related Work 2.1 Mobile GUI Agents and Their Personalized Evaluation Recent mobile GUI agents have made substantial progress in GUI perception, task planning, and multi-step task execution \citep liu2025llmpoweredguiagentsphone,nguyen-etal-2025-gui,hu-etal-2025-os. Existing systems include agent frameworks that organize task execution through explicit reasoning and control modules, such as AppAgent \citep ZhangYLLHCHF025, M3A \citep ICLR2025_01a83bc2, and Mobile-Agent-v3 \citep ye2025mobileagentv3fundamentalagentsgui, as well as end-to-end agents that directly generate reasoning traces and actions from GUI observations, such as UI-TARS \citep qin2025ui and GUI-Owl \citep ye2025mobileagentv3fundamentalagentsgui. As the GUI capabilities of these systems continue to improve, recent studies have begun to examine how agents can use user history and preferences to adapt their behavior during task execution. PersonalAlign \citep lyu-etal-2026-personalalign uses long-term user records to recover preferences omitted from vague instructions; PSPA-Bench \citep nie2026pspabenchpersonalizedbenchmarksmartphone decomposes tasks to evaluate preference-sensitive progress; KnowU-Bench \citep chen2026knowubenchinteractiveproactivepersonalized uses behavioral logs to assess preference inference, user clarification, and proactive decision-making; and Persona2Web \citep kim2026persona2webbenchmarkingpersonalizedweb studies contextual reasoning from long-term user histories in web environments. These studies broaden personalized agent evaluation from complementary directions. However, they do not jointly examine how different preferences affect GUI execution or which capabilities become bottlenecks when preferences are applied from user context to GUI actions. PrefDiag-Bench complements this line of work with an execution-oriented and stage-wise diagnostic perspective. 2.2 Personalization User Context and Memory Personalization relies on memory as a key source of user context, allowing agents to retain and reuse information from past interactions \citep zhang2025tmlr-personalization,liu2025surveypersonalizedlargelanguage. Memory systems such as MemoryBank \citep DBLP:conf/aaai/ZhongGGYW24 and Mem0 \citep ChhikaraKASY25 extract, update, and retrieve user information from ongoing interactions to support long-term personalization. Corresponding benchmarks examine this process from different perspectives. PersonaMem \citep JHCLYCea25 evaluates whether models can track evolving user profiles from multi-session interaction histories and generate personalized responses accordingly. AlpsBench \citep Xiao_2026 decomposes personalized memory management into information extraction, updating, retrieval, and utilization. In mobile GUI environments, MemGUI-Bench \citep liu2026memguibenchbenchmarkingmemorymobile focuses on memory retention and use across steps, applications, and sessions.However, correctly inferring or retrieving user information does not necessarily mean that an agent can apply user preferences correctly in a GUI task. Personalized GUI agents must further connect user context with the current task and GUI state, and translate relevant preferences into concrete behaviors such as candidate selection, ranking, process control, or user interaction. PrefDiag-Bench complements these studies by comparing explicit user profiles and behavioral memory logs in GUI tasks and probing capability gaps from user-context processing to action formulation. 3 Benchmark Design PrefDiag-Bench evaluates personalized mobile GUI agents at both the task and diagnostic levels. It contains 318 end-to-end GUI tasks, including 53 Basic and 265 preference-conditioned instances and 1,664 diagnostic probes, where each end-to-end task is linked to probes constructed from the same underlying preference instance. For mobile GUI agents, however, a more direct distinction is the type of decision that each preference changes during task execution. We therefore use preferences’ primary effects on execution as our main evaluation axis, classifying each preference by the part of a personalized task’s success criterion that it directly changes. This yields five types, illustrated in Figure 1 . Specifically, as shown in the Figure 1 , Outcome preference specifies the desired outcome or final choice, such as selecting “no sugar” and “less ice” in a drink-ordering task. A Constraint preference sets conditions that a valid outcome or allowed action must satisfy, such as keeping the drink price at or below 20$. A Ranking preference specifies priorities among valid candidates, rather than determining whether a candidate satisfies a hard constraint. For example, when several stores offer the target drink, the agent should prioritize the store with the shortest delivery time and choose the cheaper store when delivery times are equal. A Process preference specifies how a task should be carried out, such as comparing the price of the same product across multiple platforms before making a choice. The final GUI state alone is insufficient to verify this requirement: the execution trajectory must also show that the prescribed procedure was followed. An Interaction preference specifies whether, when, and how the agent should interact with the user. For example, after finding a suitable item, the agent should request confirmation and add it to the cart only after the user agrees. Although both types affect the interaction trajectory, Process constrains the task procedure, whereas Interaction constrains communication with the user. A task may therefore reach the expected final state yet still violate its preference requirements if a required comparison or confirmation was skipped during execution. 3.2 Benchmark Overview and Statistics PrefDiag-Bench evaluates agents’ ability to apply user preferences across diverse mobile tasks. It comprises 53 task families, each with one Basic task and five preference-conditioned variants, yielding 318 instances (53 Basic and 265 personalized). As shown in Figure 2 (a), the tasks span seven application domains: communication, office, commerce, navigation, system settings, information retrieval, and social media. Within the diagnostic set, preference atoms also cover nine semantic categories, including workflow, user control, time and context, resource limits, and safety and privacy (Figure 2 (c)). These categories describe what preferences concern, complementing the taxonomy that distinguishes how they alter agent behavior. Formally, we define a personalized instance as 𝒯 i = ( I i , C i , E i 0 , S i ) \mathcal{T}_{i}=(I_{i},C_{i},E_{i}^{0},S_{i}) , where I i I_{i} is the instruction, C i C_{i} is the user context conveying preference p i p_{i} , E i 0 E_{i}^{0} is the initial environment state, and S i S_{i} is a deterministic success checker. The agent is required to identify the relevant preference requirements from C i C_{i} and complete the task while satisfying all of them at the appropriate stages of execution. Execution produces a trajectory τ i = ( o 1 , a 1 , … , o T , a T ) \tau_{i}=(o_{1},a_{1},\ldots,o_{T},a_{T}) of observations and actions. The checker evaluates the final state E i T E_{i}^{T} and relevant action or user–agent interaction records, returning S i ​ ( E i T , τ i ) ∈ { 0 , 1 } S_{i}(E_{i}^{T},\tau_{i})\in\{0,1\} . A result of 1 requires satisfying both the task goal and all preference-specific requirements, including any prescribed procedure or confirmation. To examine the capabilities underlying these task outcomes, we include 1,664 diagnostic probes associated with 260 preference atoms from 256 tasks with observed failures under behavioral logs (Figure 2 (b)). Each atom is the smallest preference requirement that can be diagnosed and applied independently. Across information processing, contextual reasoning, and action formulation, the probes test preference induction from logs (P1), evidence selection for a given preference (P2), task relevance (P3), state-level trigger recognition (P4), and semantic action selection for an active preference (P5). They are evaluated independently, with ground-truth prerequisites supplied when needed; This pairing connects task outcomes with tests of specific capabilities rather than describing personalization only through aggregate task success. Figure 2 : Statistics of PrefDiag-Bench. (a) Composition of end-to-end tasks across application domains. (b) Distribution of diagnostic probes across the five diagnostic stages. (c) Distribution of fine-grained preference atoms, showing the semantic diversity of user preferences covered by the benchmark. 3.3 Data Construction and Annotation We construct preference-conditioned variants from selected KnowU-Bench tasks \citep chen2026knowubenchinteractiveproactivepersonalized, inspecting their goals, application settings, and success criteria. Every resulting variant is manually reviewed. The target preference is conveyed through user context rather than restated in the instruction. We construct paired contexts by first drafting explicit user profiles with an LLM, revising and checking them with GPT-5.6 Sol, and reviewing every profile manually. Synthetic behavioral memory logs are then generated from the reviewed profiles, with four to five profile-related entries per collection, and undergo the same model-assisted revision and human review. The underlying preference, instruction, initial environment state, and success checker remain fixed across the two context forms. We derive task-linked diagnostic probes from execution failures under behavioral logs, retaining cases with valid checker results and deduplicating them across agents by task. Independently diagnosable preference requirements are separated into atoms. Probe questions, options, and reference annotations are drafted with LLM assistance and revised by humans. For P4 and P5, we use atoms with clear trigger boundaries and usable reference trajectories. P5 reference actions are extracted from successful rollouts of the corresponding tasks and represented as semantic operations. Human reviewers answer all multiple-choice probes. 4 Experiments Table 2 : End-to-end Task Success Rates (TSR, %) on PrefDiag-Bench. RQ1. How well do GUI agents satisfy different preference requirements during task execution? RQ2. What strengths and weaknesses do agents exhibit across stages of preference application? RQ3. What relationships emerge between task-level diagnostic results and end-to-end outcomes? RQ4. What effect does evidence guidance have on end-to-end task success? RQ5. What changes in performance occur under different memory construction methods? 4.1 Experimental Setup Evaluated Systems. We evaluate 11 systems. The closed-source agents are Seed-2.0-Pro \citep seed2026seed20modelcardintelligence, Claude Sonnet 4.6 \citep anthropic2026sonnet46, and Qwen3.7-Plus \citep alibaba2026qwen37plus. The open-source agents are MAI-UI-8B \citep zhou2025maiuitechnicalreportrealworld, Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking \citep abs-2511-21631, Step-GUI-4B \citep abs-2512-15431, GUI-Owl-1.5-8B-Instruct \citep xu2026mobileagentv35multiplatformfundamentalgui, and UI-Venus-1.5-8B \citep venusteam2026uivenus15technicalreport. We also evaluate two agentic workflows, M3A and T3A \citep ICLR2025_01a83bc2, both using GPT-5.4. Open-source models run on a server with eight NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs. Evaluation Protocol. All 11 systems are evaluated on 53 Basic tasks and 265 preference-conditioned tasks, the latter under both explicit user profiles and behavioral memory logs. All systems share task environments and checkers while retaining their native observation and action interfaces. Instructions, initial states, and checkers remain fixed across profile–log pairs. We report Task Success Rate (TSR) by preference type and context form. Independent P1–P5 probes are applied to the nine directly queried agents; workflows are excluded to avoid assessing only their backbone or introducing workflow-specific probe adaptations. Diagnostic results are aggregated by task, preference, and probe type: a result is correct only if all associated items are answered correctly. We report accuracy per probe type and an overall score across all task-level diagnostic results. 4.2 End-to-End Results Table 2 reports TSR on the 53 Basic tasks and the 265 preference-conditioned tasks. For each personalized task, we compare explicit user profiles with behavioral memory logs while keeping the task instruction, initial environment state, and success checker fixed. The AVG columns report the macro-average over the five preference types. Personalized tasks are more challenging to execute. All 11 systems achieve lower average TSR on preference-conditioned tasks than on Basic tasks under both forms of user context. Seed-2.0-Pro obtains the strongest personalized results, reaching 62.64% with explicit profiles and 65.66% with behavioral logs, compared with 81.13% on Basic . In contrast, Claude Sonnet 4.6 achieves the highest Basic TSR of 86.79%, but is surpassed by Seed-2.0-Pro under both personalized settings. This ranking change shows that strong general GUI execution is important, but is not sufficient for applying user preferences throughout a multi-step interaction trajectory. Figure 3 : The heatmaps show P2 Evidence Selection, P3 Relevance Selection, and P4 Trigger Recognition. Rows represent evaluated systems and columns represent the five preference types. Darker colors indicate higher task-level accuracy. Different preference types expose distinct performance patterns. Outcome is the best-performing type for 10 of the 11 systems under explicit user profiles and for all 11 systems under behavioral memory logs. At the other end, Ranking and Process emerge as recurring difficulties across systems and user-context forms. Process is the lowest-performing type for seven systems under explicit profiles and the lowest or tied-lowest type for eight systems under behavioral memory logs. Under behavioral memory logs, Qwen3.7-Plus drops from 62.26% on Outcome to 16.98% on Process, a gap of 45.28 percentage points. Ranking remains difficult even for the strongest system: Seed-2.0-Pro achieves 83.02% on Outcome but only 45.28% on Ranking under behavioral memory logs, a difference of 37.74 points. These results show that reporting only an overall personalized score would hide major differences in the execution requirements that each system can handle. The repeated difficulty on Ranking and Process is consistent with the additional candidate comparison required by Ranking and the longer execution procedure required by Process. More explicit user context is not always more effective. The profile–log comparison has no consistent direction across systems. Behavioral logs improve Seed-2.0-Pro from 62.64% to 65.66% and T3A from 24.91% to 29.44%, whereas M3A drops from 37.73% with profiles to 18.49% with logs. This contrast is notable because M3A and T3A use the same GPT-5.4 backbone, suggesting that the usefulness of a context form also depends on how the overall workflow processes user information. This pattern is consistent with the trade-off built into the two representations: profiles directly provide compact preference rules, whereas logs preserve concrete behavioral evidence but require the agent to identify which evidence is relevant. These task-level comparisons reveal performance gaps across execution requirements and context forms, but do not isolate the capabilities underlying preference application. We next examine these capabilities using independent probes constructed from failures under behavioral memory logs. 4.3 Stage-Wise Diagnostic Results Figure 3 reports task-level accuracy on P2–P4 for the nine directly evaluated agents. P1 and P5 are omitted from the heatmaps because they are near ceiling for most systems, but are included in the aggregate statistics below. Evidence selection and trigger recognition are the weakest measured stages. On the failure-derived diagnostic set, P2 Evidence Selection and P4 Trigger Recognition are the lowest-scoring stages across systems, averaging 40.06% and 39.69%, respectively, compared with 88.80% for P3 and over 98.9% for P1 and P5. Even Seed-2.0-Pro reaches only 71.48% on P2 and 58.14% on P4. Since both probes provide the target preference, these results highlight the need to improve agents’ ability to identify supporting evidence in user history and recognize when a known preference should take effect. The Thinking variant stands out among open-source agents. Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking achieves the highest accuracy among the evaluated open-source agents on both P2 and P4. On P2, it scores 69.53%, compared with 21.88% for Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct; on P4, the corresponding scores are 45.79% and 25.58%. Its P2 accuracy also approaches the 71.48% achieved by Seed-2.0-Pro and Qwen3.7-Plus, narrowing the gap with the leading closed-source systems in evidence selection.These results suggest that the Thinking variant’s reasoning capabilities contribute to its higher accuracy in evidence selection and trigger recognition. 4.4 Joint Analysis Figure 4 : Joint outcomes between end-to-end task execution and stage-wise diagnostic probes. For each system and diagnostic stage, we partition paired task-probe outcomes into four categories: TT (both pass), TF (the task passes / the probe fails), FT (the task fails / the probe passes), and FF (both fail). The distributions reveal how failures identified by individual diagnostic stages relate to failures in complete task execution. For each of the nine directly evaluated agents, we pair every task-level diagnostic result with the corresponding end-to-end outcome under behavioral memory logs. Since the diagnostic set is deduplicated across agents, a task included due to one agent’s failure may still be completed by another agent. Figure 4 partitions the eligible paired instances into four joint outcomes: both task and probe pass (TT), the task passes but the probe fails (TF), the task fails but the probe passes (FT), and both task and probe fail (FF). P2 and P4 failures frequently co-occur with task failures. P2 Evidence Selection and P4 Trigger Recognition show markedly higher joint-failure proportions than the other diagnostic stages. Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct fails both the task and its associated probe on 65.5% of P2 pairs and 61.7% of P4 pairs. The corresponding proportions are 68.1% and 51.9% for GUI-Owl-1.5-8B-Instruct, and 82.1% and 66.0% for Step-GUI-4B. These results connect the weaknesses identified by the independent probes to failures on the corresponding GUI tasks, reinforcing evidence selection and trigger recognition as important targets for improvement. 4.5 Controlled Evidence Intervention To test whether P2 Evidence Selection is an actionable bottleneck, we evaluate Seed-2.0-Pro, Qwen3.7-Plus, Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking, and Step-GUI-4B on a fixed subset of 85 tasks selected from the 265 preference-conditioned tasks. Table 3(a) compares three conditions: C0 Raw Logs uses the original logs; C1 Oracle Evidence Labels retains all entries and labels each as supporting or noise for the target preference, without changing its text or order; C2 Supporting Logs Only removes all noise entries and retains only supporting logs. C1 tests whether explicitly identifying supporting and noise logs helps execution, while C2 tests whether removing noise is more effective than retaining and labeling it. The task instruction, initial environment state, and success checker remain fixed. Evidence labeling can outperform noise removal. From C0 to C1, Seed-2.0-Pro improves from 76.47% to 83.53%, a gain of 7.06 percentage points, and Qwen3.7-Plus improves from 50.59% to 56.47%. These gains show that explicitly distinguishing supporting logs from noise can help agents complete personalized tasks. However, replacing labeled logs with supporting-only logs (C2) reduces their TSR to 81.18% and 51.76%, respectively. For these systems, identifying which logs support the preference is therefore more effective than simply discarding the rest. A possible explanation is that labeled noise provides contrastive cues about which historical behaviors should not guide the current decision, whereas deleting these entries removes those cues. Limited GUI capability may constrain intervention benefits. Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking achieves 69.53% on P2 and 45.79% on P4, but only 30.19% on Basic tasks and 12.07% on the full preference-conditioned set under behavioral logs (Table 2 ). On the 85-task intervention subset, its TSR remains low: 17.65% under C0, 16.47% under C1, and 18.82% under C2. This contrast suggests that limitations in GUI execution constrain the gains from evidence guidance, even when evidence selection is relatively strong. Step-GUI-4B also reaches only 18.82% under both C1 and C2. These results suggest that strong GUI execution is a necessary foundation for personalized task success: when an agent’s basic GUI capability is limited, even accurate preference understanding may not translate into successful end-to-end execution. By categorizing user preferences into five types and combining this categorization with a stage-wise diagnostic framework, it examines how preferences affect agent execution, when they should take effect, and where capability gaps arise.
